newsitem.title: USA: Alternative fuels make slim gain in U.S. car fuels.
newsitem.headline: Alternative fuels make slim gain in U.S. car fuels.

text.p: Alternative fuels are expected to make up 2.7 percent of the fuel used in cars and light trucks in 1997, up from 1.6 percent five years ago, the Energy Information Administration said in a recent report.
EIA estimates that in 1997 U.S. drivers will use the equivalent of 4 billion gallons of alternative fuel, including oxygenates added to gasoline, up five percent from 1995.

Consumption was growing more slowly than anticipated because some cities had opted out of using reformulated gasoline, counted as an alternative fuel. Growth in natural gas and propane vehicles had also failed to meet expectations.
About 70 percent of the alternative fuel vehicles used in 1997 would run on propane, 20 percent would operate on natural gas, and the rest on alcohol or electricity, EIA said.
The report, "Alternatives to Traditional Transportation Fuels 1995," said nationwide in 1995 there were 330,000 alternative fuel vehicles, accounting for about 0.2 percent of all light-duty vehicles.
California with 52,000 and Texas with 32,000 had the most.

About 18,000 new on-road alternative fuel vehicles were ready to be sold that year, of which about half operated on natural gas and one-third on propane. The remainder were alcohol-fueled or electric vehicles.
About 81,000 off-road alternative fuel vehicles, such as tractors, were ready to be sold in 1995.
